newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler Ohio Jeep workers approve new labor pact.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler Ohio Jeep workers approve new labor pact.

text.p: Workers at Chrysler Corp.'s Jeep plants in Toledo, Ohio, approved a new five-year labour contract that clears the way for the automaker to invest $1.2 billion in new factories, union officials said Tuesday.
Members of United Auto Workers Local 22 ratified the contract, which is separate from Chrysler's national UAW pact, by a 73 percent margin.
The pact will allow Chrysler to reduce the number of jobs at the new plants to as low as 4,600 workers from 5,400 currently, while requiring mandatory overtime under certain circumstances.

The Jeep workers also will not reach pay parity with UAW workers at other Chrysler plants for a number of months. Under the pact, which goes into effect in September, production workers will earn first-year base wages of about $19.07 an hour, about $1 less than Chrysler workers elsewhere.
UAW spokesman Bobbie Barbee attributed the high 27 percent rejection rate to the overtime provisions. "I think the major problem was the mandatory overtime. That's the major sticking point," he said.

But the new pact was a key requirement for Chrysler to follow through on its announcement last month that it would build a state-of-the-art assembly plant in Toledo to replace creaking factories that date back to 1910.
Construction of the new plant on the site of the current Stickney Avenue plant will begin in 1998, with assembly of Jeep Cherokee and Wrangler sport utility vehicles starting there in 2001.

Toledo officials also confirmed Tuesday that Chrysler will receive tax breaks and other incentives valued at $232 million, including an $86.5 million, 10-year abatement on all city property taxes, and more than $127 million in state incentives.

The package rivals some of the larger incentives offered by state and local governments to attract auto plants in recent years. In what was widely regarded as the richest such package, officials in Alabama provided German automaker Mercedes-Benz AG with $253 million in incentives for its new sport utility plant in Vance, Ala., which opened in May.
The incentive package wasn't much less than Mercedes' $300 million investment in the project, which is expected to employ a maximum of 1,500 workers.

Separately, the UAW confirmed Tuesday that an 11:59 p.m. Friday strike deadline against a General Motors Corp.'s, Ypsilanti, Mich., transmission plant, also covers a small satellite facility in Romulus, Mich., which employs about 360 people. The two plants make rear-wheel-drive transmissions and produce components for a number of other GM transmissions.
A prolonged strike could cause widespread shutdowns of GM's North American assembly operations. Talks continued Tuesday.
